chapter.title: Unit 5 Angles and Arcs in the circle (Geometry)

blocks.text: 5-1 Central Angles and Measuring Arcs
The concept of arc length. The concept of measuring an arc. How to find the relation between chords of a circle and its arcs.
Key term: Central angle
Key term: Inscribed angle
Key term: Arc
Key term: two adjacent arcs
Key term: Measuring an arc
Key term: Chord
Key term: Tangent
In the opposite figure: The two sides of angle AMB divide the circle M into two arcs:
A central angle is the angle whose vertex is the center of the circle and whose two sides are radii in the circle.
In the opposite figure we notice that:
Arc AB is opposite to the central angle AMB, and arc ACB is opposite to the central reflective angle AMB.
If angle AMB is a straight angle (AB is a diameter in circle M), then arc AB is congruent to arc ACB and each is called a semicircle.
The measure of the arc is the measure of the central angle opposite to it.
In the opposite figure: AB is a diameter in the circle M, MC ⊥ AB, m(∠AMD) = 60°.
Notice that :
The measure of arc AD equals m(∠AMD) = 60°. $m(\overset{\frown}{AD}) = m(\angle AMD) = 60^\circ$
The measure of arc CB equals m(∠CMB) = 90°. $m(\overset{\frown}{CB}) = m(\angle CMB) = 90^\circ$
The measure of arc DC equals m(∠DMC) = 30°. (Why?) $m(\overset{\frown}{DC}) = m(\angle DMC) = 30^\circ$
The measure of arc AB equals m(∠AMB) = 180°. $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\angle AMB) = 180^\circ$
The measure of the semicircle is 180° and the measure of a circle is 360°. $180^\circ, 360^\circ$
Adjacent arcs are two arcs in the same circle that have only one point in common.

For adjacent arcs AB and BC: m(AB) + m(BC) = m(ABC), so m(AB) = m(ABC) − m(BC). $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{ABC})$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{ABC}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BC})$
In the opposite figure: AB is a diameter in the circle M, m(∠AMC) = 60°, m(∠AMD) = 40°.
Arc length is a part of a circle's circumference proportional with its measure.

Arc length = (measure of the arc / measure of the circle) × circumference of the circle. $\text{arc length}=\dfrac{\text{measure of the arc}}{\text{measure of the circle}}\times \text{circumference of the circle}$
Important corollaries :
Corollary (1): In the same circle (or in congruent circles), if the measures of arcs are equal, then the lengths of the arcs are equal, and conversely.
If: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$ then: the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ = the length of $\overset{\frown}{CD}$
If: the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ = the length of $\overset{\frown}{CD}$ then: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$
Corollary (2): In the same circle (or in congruent circles), if the measures of arcs are equal, then their chords are equal in length, and conversely.
If: $m(\widehat{AB}) = m(\widehat{CD})$ then: length of $\overline{AB}$ = length of $\overline{CD}$
If: $AB = CD$ then: $m(\widehat{AB}) = m(\widehat{CD})$
In the opposite figure: $m(\widehat{AB}) = 60^\circ$ et $m(\widehat{BC}) = 80^\circ$, $m(\widehat{AD}) : m(\widehat{DC}) = 4:7$
Corollary (3): If two parallel chords are drawn in a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.
If $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two chords in circle M, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$ then: $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{BD})$.
Corollary (4): If a chord is parallel to a tangent of a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.
If $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of circle M, $\overleftrightarrow{CD}$ is a tangent at c, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overleftrightarrow{CD}$ then $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{BC})$.

lessons.title: The relation between the inscribed and central angles subtended by the same arc

blocks.text: The relation between the inscribed and central angles subtended by the same arc
How to infer the relation between the measures of the inscribed and central angles subtended by the same arc
Key term: Inscribed angle
Key term: Central angle
Inscribed angle: an angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose sides contain two chords of the circle.
In the opposite figure : Notice that :
$\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle and $\widehat{AB}$ is the arc opposite to it.
For each inscribed angle, there is one central angle subtended by the same arc.
Theorem: The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle, subtended by the same arc.
Given: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle, $\angle AMB$ is a central angle.
R.T.P.: Prove that $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$.
Proof: There are three cases to prove this theorem.
First case: If M belongs to one of the two sides of the inscribed angle.

Since $\angle AMB$ is outside $\Delta AMC$; therefore $m(\angle AMB) = m(\angle A) + m(\angle C)$ (1). Since $AM = CM$ (radii lengths), therefore $m(\angle A) = m(\angle C)$ (2). From (1) and (2) we get: $m(\angle AMB = 2\, m(\angle C)$; therefore $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$ (Q.E.D)
Corollary (1): The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the subtended arc. $m(\angle C)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$
In the opposite figure: m(∠C) = 1/2 m(∠AMB), m(∠AMB) = m(arc AB), therefore m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc AB).
Corollary (2): The inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle is a right angle.
i.e.: If the arc opposite to the inscribed angle equals the semicircle then: m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc AB). Since m(arc AB) = 180°, therefore m(∠C) = 90°.

lessons.title: Inscribed Angles Subtended by the Same Arc

blocks.text: Lesson 5-3: Inscribed Angles Subtended by the Same Arc
How to infer the relation between the inscribed angles that include equal arcs in measure
In the same circle, the measures of all inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal in measure.
In the same circle or in congruent circles, the measures of the inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are equal.
Notice that :
In the circle M, if $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF})$ then $m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$. $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF}) \Rightarrow m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$
For any two circles M and N, if $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF})$ then $m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$. $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF}) \Rightarrow m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$
Converse of the previous corollary (point 3): in the same circle or in congruent circles, inscribed angles of equal measures subtend arcs of equal measures.

The converse of theorem 2: if two angles are subtended to the same base and on the same side of it, and have the same measure, then their vertices lie on an arc of a circle and the base is a chord in it.
In the opposite figure, notice that: ∠C, ∠D are both drawn on the base AB, and on one side of it, m(∠C) = m(∠D). Then: The points A, B, C and D lie on one circle where AB is a chord in it.

blocks.text: Cyclic Quadrilaterals (Lesson 5-4)
What you'll learn: The concept of the cyclic quadrilateral. Identifying when the shape is cyclic quadrilateral.
Key term: Cyclic quadrilateral
A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices belong to one circle.
The figure ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral because its vertices A, B, C and D belong to the circle M.

The figure XYZL is a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠YXZ) = m(∠YLZ): they are two drawn angles on the base YZ and in one direction of it, so a circle can be drawn passing through the points X, Y, Z and L, i.e. the vertices of figure XYZL belong to one circle. $m(\angle YXZ)=m(\angle YLZ)$

blocks.text: Lesson 5-5: Properties of Cyclic Quadrilaterals
What you'll learn: Properties of the cyclic quadrilateral shape. How to solve problems on the Properties of the cyclic quadrilateral shape.
Key term: Cyclic quadrilateral
In the opposite figure :
Theorem 3: In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary.
Given: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. R.T.P: Prove that: (1) m(∠A) + m(∠C) = 180°; (2) m(∠B) + m(∠D) = 180°
Proof: since m(∠A) = 1/2 m(arc BCD), and m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc BAD), therefore m(∠A) + m(∠C) = 1/2 [m(arc BCD) + m(arc BAD)] = 1/2 × 360° = 180°. Similarly: m(∠B) + m(∠D) = 180° (Q.E.D.)
Corollary: The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

In the opposite figure: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, E ∈ ray AB, E ∉ segment AB. ∴ ∠EBC is an angle outside the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠D is the inner angle opposite to it. Thus: m(∠EBC) = m(∠D) (The supplements of one angle is equal in measure)
Converse of theorem 3: If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic.
In the opposite figure: if $m(\angle A)+m(\angle C)=180^\circ$ or $m(\angle B)+m(\angle D)=180^\circ$, so ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.
Corollary: If the measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a quadrilateral figure is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex, then the figure is a cyclic quadrilateral.

In the opposite figure: ABCD is a quadrilateral, E ∈ ray AB, E ∉ segment AB. ∴ ∠EBC is an exterior angle at a vertex of the quadrilateral ABCD and ∠D is the inner angle opposite to it. If m(∠EBC) = m(∠D) then ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

lessons.title: The relation between the tangents of a circle

blocks.text: What you'll learn: How to infer the relation between the two tangent segments drawn from a point outside the circle. The concept of a circle inscribed in a polygon. How to infer the relation lon the relation between the tangents of a circle.
Key term: Chord of tangency
Key term: A circle inscribed in a polygon
Key term: Common tangents
The relation between the tangents of a circle
You know that the two tangents drawn at the two ends of a diameter in a circle are parallel.

In the opposite figure: Notice that: If AB is a chord in circle M, then the two tangents L1 and L2 intersect at the point C. Both CA and CB are called a tangent line segment and AB is called a chord of tangency.
Theorem 4: The two tangent segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length.
Given: A is a point outside the circle M, AB and AC are two tangent segments of the circle at B and C. R.T.P: Prove that: AB = AC. Construction: Draw MB, MC and MA.
Proof: ∵ AB is a tangent segment to circle M ∴ m(∠ABM) = 90°. ∵ AC is a tangent segment to circle M ∴ m(∠ACM) = 90°.
Theorem corollaries:
The straight line passing through the center of the circle and the intersection point of the two tangents is an axis of symmetry to the chord of tangency of those two tangents.
In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangents to circle M at B and C. Then: line AM is the axis of BC. Thus: AM ⊥ BC, and BD = CD

The straight line passing through the center of the circle and the intersection point of its two tangents bisects the angle between these two tangents. It also bisects the angle between the two radii passing through the two points of tangency.
In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangents to the circle M at B and C. Then: ray AM bisects ∠A, ∴ m(∠BAM) = m(∠CAM), ray MA bisects ∠BMC, ∴ m(∠AMB) = m(∠AMC)
In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangent segments to the circle M, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$, $m(\angle BMD) = 130^\circ$.
The inscribed circle of a polygon is the circle which touches all of its sides internally.
M is the inscribed circle of the triangle ABC because it touches all of its sides internally at D, E and F. i.e.: The triangle ABC is drawn outside the circle M.
Common tangents of two distant circles:
(A) The line AB is called a common internal tangent to the two circles M and N because the two circles are located at two different sides of AB; also CD is an internal tangent to the two circles.
Notice that the segments AB and CD intersect at E. $\overline{AB}\cap\overline{CD}=\{E\}$
(B) The line AB is called a common external tangent to the two circles M and N because the two circles are located in the same side of AB; also CD is an external tangent to the two circles.
Notice that the rays AB and CD intersect at F. $\overrightarrow{AB}\cap\overrightarrow{CD}=\{F\}$

blocks.text: Angles of Tangency (Lesson 5-7)

The concept of the angle of tangency; How to infer the relation between the angle of tangency and the inscribed angle subtended by the same arc; The relation between the angle of tangency and the centeral angle subtended by the same arc; How to solve problems on angels of tangency.
Key term: Angle of tangency
Key term: Inscribed angle
Key term: Central angle

In the opposite figure: $\angle ABC$ is an inscribed angle with the two sides $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and arc $AC$, $\overrightarrow{BD}$ is a tangent to the circle at B. If we imagine the revolution of one of the sides of the inscribed angle, let it be $\overrightarrow{BC}$ moving away from $\overrightarrow{BA}$ so, it takes one of the positions $\overrightarrow{BC_1}$, $\overrightarrow{BC_2}$, ............

Notice that: We get a larger inscribed angle in measure when $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}$ are about to be congruent. $\angle ABD$ is called the angle of tangency, it is a special case of the tangent angle:
The measure of angle ABD equals half the measure of arc ACD. $m(\angle ABD)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{ACD})$
Angle of tangency: the angle composed of the union of two rays, one a tangent to the circle and the other containing a chord of the circle passing through the point of tangency.
Thus: the measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the arc between the two sides, i.e. m(∠ABC) = 1/2 m(arc AB). $m(\angle ABC)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$
Theorem 5: The measure of the angle of tangency is equal to the measure of the inscribed angle subtended by the same arc.
Given: ∠ABC is an angle of tangency and ∠D is an inscribed angle. R.T.P: Prove that $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle D)$.

Proof: ∵ ∠ABC is an angle of tangency ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$ (1). ∵ ∠D is an inscribed angle ∴ $m(\angle D)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$ (2). From (1) and (2) we get: $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle C)$. Q.E.D.
Corollary: The measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc.

In the opposite figure: ray BC is tangent to circle M, AB is a chord of tangency. ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle D)$ (theorem). ∵ $m(\angle D)=\frac{1}{2}m(\angle AMB)$ (theorem). ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=\frac{1}{2}m(\angle AMB)$.
Important notice :
The angle of tangency is supplementary to the inscribed angle drawn on the chord of the angle of tangency and on one side of it.
i.e. angle ABC is supplementary to angle AEB. $\angle ABC$ is supplementary to $\angle AEB$

Converse of theorem 5: if a ray is drawn from one end of a chord of a circle so that the angle between this ray and the chord equals in measure the inscribed angle subtended by the chord in the alternate side, then this ray is a tangent to the circle.
i.e.: If we draw ray AD from one end of the chord AB in circle M and m(∠DAB) = m(∠C) then: ray AD is a tangent to circle M.
